A2.text:
Tural has a small coffee shop in Icherisheher. His sister, Leyla, helps him on weekends. Tural makes great coffee, but he uses hundreds of plastic cups every day.

One Saturday, Leyla looked at the big rubbish bin. “Tural, this is bad for nature,” she said. “These single-use cups create a lot of pollution. We must go green.”

“I know,” Tural said. “But glass cups are expensive to wash. And people want to take their coffee outside to the Boulevard.”

“We can ask people to bring their own cups,” Leyla answered. “We can give them a cheaper price. Also, we can recycle our paper and plastic.”

Tural was not sure. “Will people really do that?”

“Let's try,” she smiled.

On Monday, Tural put a big sign on the door. It said: “Bring your cup, pay less!”

At first, nobody cared. But on Wednesday, a young man brought a red metal cup. Then, two students brought their own mugs. By Friday evening, the rubbish bin was only half full.

Tural was very surprised. “You were right,” he told Leyla. “It is a small change, but it helps. Next week, I want to buy wooden spoons too!”

Leyla laughed loudly. “Good job! We are saving the world, one coffee at a time.”

B1.text:
Tural runs a popular coffee shop in Icherisheher. His younger sister, Leyla, studies environmental science and helps him on weekends. Tural's coffee is famous, but his business has a big problem. He throws away hundreds of plastic cups every single day.

One Saturday afternoon, Leyla looked at the overflowing rubbish bins outside. “Tural, we really have to stop this,” she said. “These single-use plastics cause terrible pollution. If we want to reduce our carbon footprint, we need to turn over a new leaf.”

Tural sighed and wiped the counter. “Leyla, I own one tiny cafe in Baku. Even if I stop using plastic entirely, it is just a drop in the ocean. Plus, paper cups cause deforestation. What should I do?”

“We can encourage customers to bring their own reusable cups,” Leyla suggested. “If they do, we will give them a ten percent discount. We can also recycle everything we use in the shop.”

Tural thought it was a strange idea, but he agreed to try it for a week.

On Monday morning, Tural put a chalkboard outside. The sign explained the new discount. For the first two days, people ignored it. But on Wednesday, a regular customer came in with a beautiful ceramic mug. On Thursday, a group of office workers brought their own flasks.

By the end of the week, Tural noticed something amazing. He had only used half the amount of plastic cups he normally used. He also saved money on buying them.

“You were completely right,” Tural admitted to his sister on Sunday. “It actually works. Next month, I want to buy our electricity from a renewable energy provider.”

Leyla smiled proudly. “See? A small drop can create a big wave.”

questions.why: He feels that because he owns just one tiny cafe, his actions won't make a real difference to global pollution.

B2.text:
Tural managed a thriving artisan coffee shop nestled in the winding streets of Icherisheher. While his espresso was widely considered the best in town, the café had a glaring flaw. Every day, it generated mountains of waste. His sister Leyla, a university student passionate about sustainability, often helped out on weekends and never missed a chance to critique his habits.

One busy Saturday, Leyla dragged Tural to the back alley, pointing at the overflowing bins. “Look at this,” she scolded. “Our reliance on single-use plastics is a disaster for local biodiversity and creates needless pollution. If you are serious about lowering your carbon footprint, it is time to turn over a new leaf.”

Tural leaned against the ancient stone wall and sighed. “Leyla, I run a single, independent cafe in a huge city. Even if I completely eradicate plastic from my shop, it’s just a drop in the ocean. And switching to paper isn't much better, considering the impact of deforestation.”

“Every effort counts,” Leyla countered, refusing to back down. “We can launch a green initiative. Let's offer a twenty percent discount to anyone who brings a reusable cup. We can also rigorously recycle our waste. Just give it a shot for a fortnight.”

Though highly skeptical, Tural finally surrendered. On Monday morning, an elegant wooden sign was placed by the door, boldly advertising the eco-friendly discount.

Initially, the regulars barely noticed. However, by midweek, the tide began to turn. A young lawyer arrived with a sleek metal thermos, and soon, a group of university students followed suit with colourful travel mugs. Tural was astonished to see people actively participating.

When Friday evening rolled around, Tural did the inventory. The results were undeniable: he had used sixty percent fewer disposable cups and significantly reduced his overhead costs.

“I have to eat my words,” Tural confessed on Sunday morning, pouring Leyla a fresh latte. “It was a phenomenal success. In fact, I've been researching how we can switch our shop's power supply to a renewable energy provider next year.”

Leyla took a sip and beamed. “I told you. When enough people care, it’s no longer a drop in the ocean.”

words.phrase: give it a shot for a fortnight

questions.q: What message does the story convey?
options: That running a coffee shop is impossible without plastic
That family members should not work together
That collective small efforts can significantly impact environmental sustainability
That large corporations are responsible for most pollution
questions.why: The story shows how a small, local initiative reduced waste, proving that when enough people care, it makes a real difference.

options: The espresso was too bitter
The stone walls were falling apart

The coffee was too expensive
questions.why: “...the café had a glaring flaw. Every day, it generated mountains of waste.”

questions.q: What specific incentive did they offer to change customer behaviour?
options: A free coffee after ten purchases
A larger cup of coffee for the same price
Free wooden spoons and sugar

questions.why: “Let's offer a twenty percent discount to anyone who brings a reusable cup.”

questions.q: Tural agreed to Leyla's idea enthusiastically from the very beginning.
options: True
False

questions.why: “Though highly skeptical, Tural finally surrendered.” He was not enthusiastic at first.

questions.q: Leyla says they need to “turn over a new leaf”. What does this idiom mean?
options: To start behaving in a better and more responsible way
To close the shop and open a new one
To pick up leaves from the street
To change the menu completely
questions.why: She wants Tural to change his environmentally harmful habits and start acting more sustainably.

questions.q: What does Tural mean when he says “I have to eat my words”?
options: He is very hungry after a long week
He admits that his previous doubts about the idea were completely wrong
He wants to stop talking and drink his latte
He is angry that Leyla forced him to change
questions.why: He previously thought it was a useless idea (“a drop in the ocean”), but after seeing it work, he admits he was wrong.

podcast.title: One bag at a time

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: How many plastic bags or bottles did you use this week? Guess: who in this episode started a big green project at home — Leyla or Sam?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today we're talking about the environment — and I did an experiment.
Oh, I love experiments. What was it?
For one week I kept every piece of plastic I used. Every bottle, every bag, every coffee cup. [sigh] By Sunday my kitchen table was full.
Full? In one week?
Yes. And most of it was single-use. I used it for five minutes and then threw it away.
That's the problem, isn't it? Plastic lives for hundreds of years. Pollution in the sea is terrible now.
So I decided to turn over a new leaf. Now I carry a cloth bag and my own bottle.
Good for you! But some people say: 'One person can't change anything. It's just a drop in the ocean.'
I hear that a lot. And it's true that the big changes must come from countries and companies.
Like renewable energy — sun and wind instead of oil and gas.
Exactly. And stopping deforestation. When we cut down forests, we lose biodiversity — thousands of animals and plants.
And the forests take carbon from the air. So every tree matters.
But I still think small actions count. If a million people do one small thing, it's not small any more.
I agree. My family started to recycle last year. Paper, glass and plastic in different bins.
Was that difficult?
At first, yes. [chuckle] My dad put everything in the wrong bin for a month. Now he checks everyone else's!
[laugh] The new environmental police. Do you think about your carbon footprint too?
A little. I take the metro more and I fly less. For me, sustainability means asking: do I really need this?
That's a great question. Buy less, buy better, use it longer. That's how we go green without stress.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what is one thing you could do this week for the planet?
Mine is no more coffee cups. See you next time!
Bye for now!
